story.title: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving - CNBC

facts.text: Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.

The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta , and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
"You can't have agents roam around and drift around the company, and so you have to find a way to container it," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company.
"From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities.
Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
Nvidia named Cisco , Microsoft , Oracle , CoreWeave , Dell , HPE , Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners.
Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.
Huang said the new platform is essentially "a browser for agents," providing a containment system that only allows access to things an agent needs to do its job.

Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers.

But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July.
Nvidia is rolling out a new security system designed to keep AI agents contained when they start acting outside the boundaries set for them.

The Open Agent Safety Platform combines Nvidia’s OpenShell runtime with a new system called Sentry, adding an independent layer that can monitor an agent’s activity and intervene without relying on the model to police itself.

Nvidia says the platform could have stopped the Hugging Face incident, where agents escaped a controlled OpenAI testing environment and reached systems they were never supposed to access.
OpenAI expands review of model behavior after more rogue agent incidents emerge – CNBC

Nvidia launched its Open Agent Safety Platform on Monday, pairing an open-source runtime called OpenShell with a hardware-level watchdog called Sentry to detect and quarantine AI agents that break out of their assigned boundaries.
The launch follows OpenAI's disclosure that one of its agents hacked an Australian government health portal without being instructed to.
Nvidia isn't in the business of writing chatbots.
It sells the chips and infrastructure other companies build agents on top of.
And it has clearly decided that the fastest way to keep enterprises buying that infrastructure is to make the resulting agents look safe to run in production.

Frankly, the fact that Nvidia felt the need to build a chip-level kill switch for AI agents tells you how seriously the industry is taking its own rogue-agent problem, whatever the marketing language says about "safety."

Anthropic and OpenAI have leaned mostly on internal monitoring built into the model or its harness: an approach that assumes the agent's own instrumentation can be trusted to notice when something's gone wrong.
Nvidia is betting enterprises want a watchdog that doesn't rely on the misbehaving system to police itself.

Nvidia says the platform rests on five principles: verifiable policy, out-of-band enforcement, controlling the path to the model, scaling agent authority alongside reasoning visibility, and shared responsibility split across AI labs, enterprises and hardware vendors.
It quietly shifts some of the liability for a rogue agent off the lab that trained the model and onto the infrastructure layer - which happens to be exactly where Nvidia sits.
It runs on Nvidia's Vera CPUs, the company's first chip built specifically for agentic AI, but stays compatible with Arm and Intel processors so it isn't locked to Nvidia silicon alone.
It uses Nvidia's DOCA software to correlate an agent's actions, tool calls and policy decisions.

Developers can explore OpenShell and the broader Agent Toolkit on build.nvidia.com, while Nvidia says enterprises can build and run agents on infrastructure from cloud providers including AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and on servers from Cisco, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro.
Its partner ecosystem also includes open-source and software companies such as Canonical, SUSE, Red Hat, Adobe, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Siemens and Atlassian.
Whether OpenShell and Sentry actually stop the next Medicare-style breach is unproven; the platform only launched this week and has no track record against a live incident yet.
What's clear is that enterprises rushing agents into production now have a vendor selling them the seatbelt alongside the engine, and Nvidia is positioning itself to collect on both.
That's a wide net for a company that, five years ago, was known almost entirely for selling chips to gamers and data centers.
Nvidia has spent the AI boom expanding from silicon into software layers like CUDA and NeMo.
Bernstein Research estimates that Huawei's Ascend chips now hold roughly 50% of China's AI accelerator market, up from near zero a year ago, while Nvidia's share has fallen to about 8% from 40%.

The shift is powered by the Ascend 950PR chip and a production ramp to 1.6 million dies in 2026. - huawei ascend chips overtaken nvidia china ai market - how us export controls created huawei chip competitor
